extracted.intended_audience: general readers of literary non‑fiction / students of criminal history and true crime
extracted.subtask_description: A literary non‑fiction essay recounting the investigation and trial of Hélène Jegado (19th‑century poisonings), discussing evidence, witness testimony, medical opinion, and social context. The page mixes reportage of facts with commentary on legal procedure and human motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescription légale (statute_of_limitations) limiting charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the prescription legale twenty‑three poisonings, six attempts at poisoning, and a number of thefts, all of which had taken place within the space of ten years, had to be left out of the indictment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal time limits can remove many alleged incidents from formal charges, but investigative and narrative attention to those incidents may still be admissible or considered by the court informally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible evidence in French criminal trials (admission of hearsay)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes 'those curious samples of “what the soldier said” that are so often admitted in French criminal trials as evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French practice at the time allowed certain hearsay or community‑reported statements to be admitted, so testimony of bystanders or 'what was said' could influence proceedings even if it would be inadmissible under stricter Anglo‑Saxon rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited formal role of scientific experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific experts could be called only to assist the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts are available to the court for assistance rather than adversarial determinative authority; the court still weighs expert testimony among other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of autopsy / post‑mortem for proving poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors pressed for an autopsy (post‑mortem) to determine cause of death, but peasant relatives often refused; lack of autopsy impaired certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A post‑mortem can provide definitive pathological evidence (e.g., arsenic in viscera). Refusal or absence of autopsy often leaves medical opinion inconclusive and weakens definitive proof of poisoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical analysis of viscera as decisive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The President states: 'Chemical analysis has proved the presence of arsenic in the viscera of Perrotte.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical detection of poison in organs is treated as strong, objective evidence linking death to arsenical poisoning and can anchor circumstantial testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive (or its absence) as a factor in detection and suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a commonplace that murder without motive is the hardest to detect. Helene's earlier crimes are described as 'quite lacking in discoverable motive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a clear motive makes it harder for contemporaries and investigators to suspect and pursue a person; motive often dictates the intensity of scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterned symptoms, relapses, and clinical course suggesting poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors initially misdiagnosed illnesses; victims showed sudden relapses, vomiting, purging, abdominal pain, distension, swelling of feet—symptoms later thought consistent with arsenical poisoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unusual clinical pattern (mild initial signs followed by sudden deterioration, relapses, specific gastrointestinal symptoms) should raise suspicion of poisoning and prompt chemical/forensic investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outward piety and attentiveness can mask culpability (character evidence effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Helene's piety and tender care often disarmed suspicion; her religious observances and attentions made people trust her despite rumours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal reputation for piety or devoted care may bias witnesses and investigators, reducing suspicion even when circumstantial evidence accumulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent theft or pilfering increases plausibility of guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Helene had neglected to combine her poisoning with detected pilfering the people about her victims could see nothing wrong; where thefts were discovered, suspicion grew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery of thefts provides a tangible, provable wrongdoing that can corroborate other suspicions and prompt closer inquiry into unexplained deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated prophetic or predicting remarks by accused as circumstantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses reported Helene saying of sufferers that 'she'll never get better' or 'she's a lost woman'; such predictions were noted and used against her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrent statements by an accused foretelling or minimizing recovery of ill persons may be considered suspicious circumstantial behaviour, especially when followed by decline or death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and limits of witness testimony about behaviour and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous witnesses recounted Helene's habits (drinking, secret eating, not dining with others), reputation ('white liver'), and specific acts (stowing a packet, stealing wine), which informed the court's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witness accounts of demeanour, reputation, and small acts can build a cumulative case, but individual reports may be unreliable and are strongest when corroborated by physical or medical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical possession or discovery of suspect substances as key evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention is made of packets found in a chest at Locsine and of a white powder seen in Helene's possession; it was never clearly established they contained arsenic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct physical evidence of possession of poisons or related paraphernalia is highly probative, but ambiguity or inability to chemically identify the substance weakens its evidentiary value.
